summary: Defined a bit-string label for DNS names so records could be stored at any bit boundary in a binary-named part of the tree. It is historic, with RFC 6891 listed as replacing it.

plainLanguage.summary: A scheme for naming by single bits instead of whole words. It was tried but dropped, and is now historic.

questions: what is a dns bit string label
how many bits fit in a bit string label
what is a one bit label
subtitle: A DNS label type that packs a run of single-bit labels together, so names can be split at any bit boundary.

tldr.problem: When a name space is most naturally written in binary, ordinary DNS labels make it hard to store data and delegate authority at arbitrary bit boundaries.
tldr.mechanism: A Bit-String Label groups up to 256 One-Bit Labels into one label, with a count, the bits, and a defined text form and sort order.
tldr.outcome: This RFC is now Historic. It was updated by RFC 3363 and RFC 3364 and obsoleted by RFC 6891.

today: RFC 2673 is Historic. It was updated by RFC 3363 and RFC 3364 and obsoleted by RFC 6891. It updated RFC 1035.

sections.title: The Problem and the Idea
sections.content:
RFC 2673 defines a Bit-String Label that may appear within domain names. It compactly stands for a sequence of One-Bit Labels, and it lets resource records be stored at any bit boundary in a binary-named section of the domain name tree.

The goal is to store data and delegate authority on arbitrary boundaries when the name space is most naturally represented in binary.
sections.plainLanguage: Some things, like numbers, are really strings of 0s and 1s. This lets DNS name them one bit at a time instead of by whole words.

sections.title: The Wire Format
sections.content:
Up to 256 One-Bit Labels fit in one Bit-String Label. The label starts with the two bits 01, then a six-bit extended label type (ELT) of 000001 binary, then a one-octet Count, then the Label bits.

Count is the number of significant bits. A value of zero means 256 bits, which makes a zero-bit label impossible. The bits go most significant first, padded on the right with zero to seven pad bits to fill whole octets. Pad bits MUST be zero on transmission and ignored on reception.

A sequence of bits may be split across several Bit-String Labels, and the division points have no significance.
sections.plainLanguage: The label says how many bits it holds, then lists them. Any spare space at the end is filled with zeros that everyone ignores.

sections.title: The Text Form
sections.content:
In a zone file, a Bit-String Label is written as a bit specification between \[ and ]. The specification is a dotted quad or a base indicator (b, o or x for base 2, 8 or 16) followed by digits, optionally followed by a slash and a length.

The length must be between 1 and 32 after a dotted quad, or between 1 and 256 otherwise. Insignificant bits in a final digit MUST be zero, and machine-generated text SHOULD give the length explicitly.

The RFC shows four spellings of the same label: \[b11010000011101], \[o64072/14], \[xd074/14] and \[208.116.0.0/14].
sections.plainLanguage: You can write the same bit pattern in several ways, like writing the same number in decimal or hexadecimal. The result means the same thing.

sections.title: Canonical Form, Sorting and Matching
sections.content:
For DNS signature records to work, binary labels must be in a predictable canonical form. That form uses the fewest possible Bit-String Labels, and all except possibly the first (least significant) label are of maximum length. For example, a sequence of 513 to 768 One-Bit Labels has three Bit-String Labels, of which the second and third hold 256 label bits.

For sorting, any One-Bit Label sorts before any standard label, and a 0 bit sorts before a 1 bit. A One-Bit Label never matches any other kind of label, so the ASCII labels 0 and 1 do not match bit values 0 and 1.
sections.plainLanguage: To compare two names fairly, everyone must pack the bits the same way, and zeros must come before ones.

sections.title: IANA and Security Notes
sections.content:
The RFC defines one Extended Label Type, the Bit-String Label, and requests code point 000001 binary in the space defined by RFC 2671 (EDNS0).

On security, all considerations that apply to ordinary ASCII DNS labels apply equally to binary labels, and the canonicalization and sorting rules let DNS Security address them.
sections.plainLanguage: The new label kind gets its own number in an official list. It needs the same safety care as normal DNS names.
